question: Who may offer sacrifices to God?
summary: The Priestly legislation in Numbers 18 and Leviticus 17 restricts sacrifice to Aaronide priests at the tabernacle door, threatening death for any layperson who slaughters away from that one altar. But 1 Samuel happily reports Samuel — an Ephraimite, not a Levite — offering a burnt offering at Mizpah, and YHWH answers him without complaint.

reconcile.connective: Defenders read Samuel's offering as a recognized exception — a non-priest acting under prophetic warrant and the necessity of a destroyed sanctuary, not a breach of the altar law.

discrepancy.connective: Julius Wellhausen presses the sharpest form of the objection, arguing the Priestly restriction of sacrifice to Aaronide priests at one altar is a late, post-exilic construction that the older Samuel narratives know nothing of — so the two cannot both reflect the same law.

excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Though Samuel was not a priest, yet he offered this sacrifice … His not sacrificing at the tabernacle was justified by the necessity of the case; neither tabernacle nor ark was at hand.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly concedes Samuel was not a priest and that he sacrificed away from the tabernacle, then offers the harmonizing ground (necessity, no tabernacle/ark at hand) — squarely on the priest-only/one-altar tension.
excerpts.source_note_text:
Samuel took a sucking lamb - This sucking lamb must have been eight days under its mother before it could be offered, as the law says, Lev 22:27.
Though Samuel was not a priest, yet he offered this sacrifice; or he might have ordered Eleazar to offer it, and still be said to have done it himself: Qui facit per alterum, facit per se; "He who procures a thing to be done, may be said to do it himself." His not sacrificing at the tabernacle was justified by the necessity of the case; neither tabernacle nor ark was at hand.
